title: Research Bite #28: Teaching to the Test
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #28 covers Muth and Luftenegger's longitudinal study of "teaching to the test" (TTT) and its effect on student motivation among 1,855 Austrian secondary students preparing for the Matura exam. Using latent change score modeling across grades 11 and 12, the researchers tracked how students' perceived exposure to TTT practices -- familiarizing students with test formats, repetitive exam-style exercises, referencing the test during lessons -- changed as the exam approached, and how that change related to shifts in intrinsic motivation, perceived importance, and utility value. Contrary to the common assumption that TTT kills motivation, the study found perceived TTT increased as the exam neared, and that increase was associated with positive changes in several motivational measures rather than negative ones. The authors are careful to caveat the finding: it comes from a single study in one national context (Austrian Gymnasium students, a low-to-medium-stakes exam), doesn't examine actual achievement, and shouldn't be read as license to abandon varied, student-centered teaching -- their own framing is that "the dose makes the poison" and TTT should be used in moderation. For teachers anxious about test-prep season undermining engagement, the practical takeaway is that strategic TTT close to a high-stakes exam is not automatically the motivation-killer it's often assumed to be.
points: The core counterintuitive finding: perceived teaching-to-the-test increased as an exam approached, and that increase tracked positive rather than negative changes in intrinsic motivation, importance, and utility value.

This is described as the first study to directly test the assumed TTT-motivation link longitudinally, rather than relying on the correlational or cross-sectional designs that dominated prior research.
The authors' own caveat -- "the dose makes the poison" -- means the findings support moderate, strategic TTT near an exam, not a wholesale shift away from varied, student-centered teaching.
The study measured perceived motivation, not actual exam achievement, so teachers should treat the result as reassurance about engagement rather than evidence that TTT improves learning outcomes.
quotes: This research article examines the impact of “teaching to the test” (TTT), a practice focusing on test preparation, on secondary school students’ motivation in Austria.
While commonly viewed negatively, this study, using longitudinal data and Expectancy-Value Theory, found that students perceived an increase in TTT closer to graduation.

Contrary to expectations, this perceived increase was linked to positive changes in intrinsic motivation, perceived importance, and utility of the subject, suggesting TTT may not be inherently detrimental.
To the authors’ knowledge, this was the first study to directly examine the association and direct effects of (perceived) TTT on student motivation.
They suggest that, as in many areas, “the dose makes the poison” and teachers should strive to provide students with a variety of teaching methods, using TTT “in moderation”.

Teaching to the test (TTT), contrary to widespread concerns, might not have the detrimental effects on student motivation that many researchers and educators fear, and can even enhance some aspects of it when used strategically before exams
The study focused on motivation and did not investigate the effects of TTT on students’ actual achievement in the final exam.
